name: localtunnel (client) / localtunnel-server
weekly_downloads_or_stars: localtunnel npm: 408 dependents, 33 versions (client pkg last published 5 years ago); server repo: 3.3k GitHub stars, 1.1k forks
last_published_date: localtunnel client v2.0.2 published ~5 years ago (stale); server repo also largely dormant
maturity_notes: Widely known (the original 'ngrok alternative'), but effectively unmaintained for years. Uses a bespoke HTTP-based tunnel protocol (client opens a raw TCP/HTTP connection to server, not literally a browser WebSocket) rather than the ws upgrade handshake. Server requires wildcard DNS (*.domain.tld) and listening on arbitrary OS-assigned TCP ports per client — architecturally heavier than embedding into an existing Express/SvelteKit HTTP listener.
what_it_actually_does: THIS IS the closest real match to the reverse-tunnel pattern: client makes an outbound connection to the tunnel server, server assigns a public subdomain, and inbound HTTP requests to that subdomain are forwarded down the persistent connection to the client, which relays them to a local port. However, the transport is a raw TCP socket via Node's 'net' module (HTTP CONNECT-style), not a WebSocket, and the server is a full standalone service (needs its own port range, DNS wildcarding) rather than a small piece of middleware droppable into an existing HTTP server's request handler.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: High. localtunnel-server is not designed to run as embedded Express middleware — it's a standalone server.js process with its own port-per-client allocation logic and required wildcard subdomain DNS. Bolting this into an adapter-node SvelteKit app would mean running a second process alongside SvelteKit and reverse-proxying to it, not a clean 20-line integration. Realistically 200+ lines of adaptation work and infra changes (DNS, port ranges) if you tried to fold its logic in-process.
client_side_requirements: There IS an existing Node.js client library (npm 'localtunnel'), but no official Python client. Go and C#/.NET community clients exist (gotunnelme, go-localtunnel, localtunnel-client for .NET) but no Python one was found. Would need to reverse-engineer/reimplement the wire protocol in Python.
viability_notes: Conceptually the right pattern but wrong transport (raw TCP, not WS) and wrong deployment shape (standalone server needing wildcard DNS + dynamic port allocation, not embeddable middleware). Would require significant rework to embed in an existing SvelteKit/Node server and to write a Python client from scratch since the wire protocol isn't WebSocket-based.

name: tunnelmole
license: AGPL-3.0 (tunnelmole-service, per project docs) / client package license not explicitly restated on npm page
weekly_downloads_or_stars: npm: 17 dependents, 92 versions; GitHub client repo stars in the low hundreds to low thousands range (exact count not captured from this page)
maturity_notes: Open-source 'ngrok alternative', actively marketed, has a hosted service plus a self-hostable server (tunnelmole-service). More recently maintained than localtunnel. Also importable/embeddable as a Node dependency to programmatically start a tunnel client (not server) inside your own app.
what_it_actually_does: Same tunnel-through-NAT pattern as localtunnel: client connects outbound to tunnelmole's server, gets assigned a public URL, and the server relays inbound HTTP to the client which forwards to a local port. The npm package published here is the CLIENT half; the reverse-tunnel SERVER piece is a separate, self-hostable repo (tunnelmole-service), not documented in this fetch as an embeddable middleware — appears to be a standalone service like localtunnel-server.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: The client side is trivial to embed (a few lines: `import {tunnelmole} from 'tunnelmole'; await tunnelmole({port})`), but that's the wrong side for our use case (we need the SERVER logic embedded in the SvelteKit backend, not the client). The tunnelmole-service (server) was not confirmed to be embeddable middleware; treat as a standalone service similar to localtunnel-server — likely comparable integration cost (100+ lines / separate process).
client_side_requirements: Existing npm/Node client only; no Python client. The end-user's local machine would need Node.js and this npm package, OR we'd need to write a Python client implementing the same wire protocol as tunnelmole-service (protocol details not verified in this pass).
viability_notes: Good UX and more recently maintained than localtunnel, but the reusable/embeddable piece here is the CLIENT (Node-only), which is the wrong side for us since our need is a Python client talking to an embedded server library. The actual tunnel SERVER (tunnelmole-service) wasn't confirmed as embeddable middleware.

name: http-proxy (node-http-proxy, http-party)
weekly_downloads_or_stars: 3,347 dependents on npm (very widely used); underlying GitHub repo has tens of thousands of stars (http-party/node-http-proxy)
last_published_date: v1.18.1 published ~6 years ago (stable/mature, low churn)
maturity_notes: Extremely mature and battle-tested generic HTTP/WS proxy library, embeddable via `proxy.web(req,res,{target})` and `proxy.ws(req,socket,head,{target})`.
what_it_actually_does: DOES NOT FIT the reverse-tunnel pattern. This is a generic forward reverse-proxy: given a known target URL (e.g. http://localhost:9000), it forwards HTTP or WebSocket-upgrade requests to that target. It has no concept of a persistent client-initiated tunnel connection through which arbitrary requests get multiplexed to a NAT'd client — it assumes the proxy process already has direct network access to the target. Not usable as-is for tunneling through firewalls/NAT.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: N/A for our use case — would only be relevant as a building block if paired with custom multiplexing logic on top, not as a drop-in tunnel solution. As a plain reverse proxy it's ~10-20 lines to wire into Express, but that's not what we need.
client_side_requirements: None — it's server-only and assumes the target is directly reachable, which is exactly the constraint we don't have (client is behind NAT/firewall).
viability_notes: Included because it repeatedly surfaces in 'websocket reverse proxy npm' searches, but it is explicitly the generic-proxy case the task warned about — not a NAT-traversal reverse-tunnel tool. Not viable for APLC-1 replacement, though its `ws()` proxying code could inform how to plumb WS upgrades if we build our own.

name: primus
maturity_notes: Mature, long-lived abstraction layer over multiple realtime transports (ws, engine.io, SockJS, uws, etc.) with built-in reconnect/heartbeat protocol (`primus::ping`/`primus::pong`). Has real protocol documentation making a from-scratch client feasible.
what_it_actually_does: DOES NOT implement the reverse-tunnel/HTTP-multiplexing pattern. It's a real-time messaging abstraction (like Socket.IO) for building bidirectional pub/sub or RPC-style apps over WebSockets with automatic reconnect — not a mechanism for exposing a NAT'd local HTTP server to the public internet or multiplexing arbitrary HTTP requests down a single socket to a specific backend.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Trivial to attach to an existing http.Server (`new Primus(server, options)`), roughly 5-10 lines, but doesn't solve the tunneling/multiplexing problem — would only be useful as the transport layer if we build APLC-1 ourselves on top of it (handles reconnect/heartbeat framing for us).
client_side_requirements: No Python client exists; Primus's client is JS-only (browser or Node). Its documented text protocol (`primus::ping::<epoch>`, `primus::pong::<epoch>`, etc.) is simple enough that a Python client COULD be hand-written against it if we chose to build our own tunnel logic using Primus purely as the reconnecting-transport layer.
viability_notes: Useful as a reconnect/heartbeat transport primitive to borrow from, not as a ready-made reverse-tunnel solution. Would still require us to build the entire request-multiplexing/routing logic (i.e., most of APLC-1) on top of it ourselves.

name: yamux (npm)
maturity_notes: Essentially abandoned toy/proof-of-concept implementation of a stream multiplexer, requires Node v0.10.x (ancient). Not usable in a modern project.
what_it_actually_does: It IS a genuine stream-multiplexing library (create N virtual duplex streams over one shared channel, matching the general shape needed for multiplexing many HTTP requests down one WebSocket) — conceptually the right primitive — but it is not integrated with WebSockets, HTTP, or any tunnel-server semantics; you'd have to build the HTTP-over-multiplexed-stream layer, the WS transport wiring, and the auth/routing entirely yourself. Also unmaintained for over a decade and not compatible with modern Node.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Not usable as-is (incompatible with modern Node); would need to find a modern replacement (e.g. reimplement HashiCorp's real 'yamux' protocol, which this npm package is NOT actually related to despite the name) or use another multiplexing lib.
client_side_requirements: N/A — package is effectively dead. Note also that this npm package has no relation to HashiCorp's actual Yamux multiplexing protocol used in libp2p/consul despite sharing the name; there is no official 'yamux' npm implementation of that real protocol either.
viability_notes: Dead package, wrong/misleading name-match to the real Yamux protocol, requires Node 0.10. Not usable. Confirms there is no mature, modern npm library implementing true stream multiplexing-over-WebSocket ready to embed.
